title: A green gate doesn't predict a clean review
statement: Don't expect a gate on which every check passes to predict a clean review: most findings on green lessons needed human judgment that no check could supply.
example: Of 26 review findings on lessons whose checks were all green, 3 later became machine-checkable and 23 stayed human calls.
detail: A reading course kept a calibration log to test whether a green gate predicts that review finds nothing, matching each review round with the state of the course's checks when the review happened. On 5 rows where every check was green, 26 findings landed: 3 have since become machine-checkable, a check on where the key sits and a cap on task-opener length, and 23 remained human calls, such as layout taste, sibling questions whose answers crack each other, where audio marks fall, whether a story frame makes sense and whether a word-part gloss is right. A further 29 findings, on lessons whose checks were not yet green, were all mismatches between a design document and the shipped lesson, which no check in the course compared.
against: The gate state at each review was reconstructed afterwards from commit messages rather than recorded at the time, and the log holds only 9 rows from a few lessons (`grade3-reading/artifacts/calibration/ROUNDS.md`, lines 16-27, 51 and 101-112).

evidence.quote: **26 findings landed on lessons whose gate was green at review time** (5 rows: L4/L5 @ 27.08, arc-level sim-review @ 28.08, L4/L5 @ 30.08). Of those 26, **3 have since become machine-catchable**
**23 remain irreducibly human** as of this writing
Purpose: build the dataset that will eventually let us claim "gate-PASS predicts reviewers finding nothing" — honestly, which for now means mostly disproving it and measuring the gap.
